label: Camera Models
notes: This chapter, printed pages 153 through 177, builds the projective camera from scratch. We treat the camera as a single three by four matrix that maps homogeneous world points to homogeneous image points, then spend the rest of the lecture reading geometry directly off that matrix and its blocks.

label: The Basic Pinhole Camera
notes: Start with the central projection idea. A world point, the camera center, and the image point are collinear, so similar triangles give the focal-length scaling. Writing this in homogeneous coordinates linearizes the nonlinear division by depth, which is the whole reason projective coordinates earn their keep here.

label: The Camera Matrix P = K[R | t]
notes: Here is the master equation. The full finite camera factors into a calibration matrix times a rigid motion. K holds everything internal to the sensor, while R and t encode where the camera sits and how it points. Every later camera model is a constrained special case of this factorization.

label: Intrinsics: The Calibration Matrix K
notes: K is upper triangular and carries five degrees of freedom: two focal lengths in pixel units, the principal point offset, and skew. Skew is nearly zero for real CCD sensors. Aspect ratio is the ratio of the two focal entries. These parameters live entirely in the image plane and ignore world pose.

label: Extrinsics: Pose R and t
notes: The extrinsics place the camera in the world. R rotates world axes into the camera frame, and the translation satisfies t equals minus R times C. Emphasize that t is not the camera position; you must invert the rotation to recover the center C, a common source of sign and frame confusion.

label: The Camera Center
notes: The camera center is the unique point the camera cannot see, and algebraically it is the right null vector of P. Because P has rank three, its null space is one-dimensional, giving exactly one center up to scale. We verify this numerically: P times the homogeneous center returns the zero vector.

label: Principal Plane, Axis, and Point
notes: Read the rows of P geometrically. The third row is the principal plane through the center, parallel to the image plane. Its left three entries give the principal axis direction. The principal axis pierces the image plane at the principal point, which is also where the optical axis meets the sensor.

label: Columns and Rows of P
notes: The columns are vanishing points of the world coordinate axes, and the fourth column is the image of the world origin. The rows are world planes: two through image axes and one principal plane. Knowing this lets you sketch a camera's behavior without ever multiplying it out fully.

label: Forward Projection x = PX
notes: Forward projection is one matrix multiply followed by a homogeneous divide. Scaling the world point or the matrix does not change the image point, because both live in projective space. We confirm scale invariance numerically: projecting X and seven point five times X yields the identical pixel.

label: Back-Projection to a Ray
notes: A single image point does not fix depth, so back-projection returns a ray, not a point. The ray passes through the camera center and the back-projected point given by the pseudo-inverse of P. This one-to-many inverse is exactly why a second view is needed to triangulate structure.

label: Cameras at Infinity: Affine Models
notes: Push the camera center to infinity and perspective division disappears. The result is the affine camera family: orthographic, weak perspective, and para-perspective. Their bottom row is fixed at zero zero zero one, so parallel world lines stay parallel in the image. They are linear approximations valid for shallow, distant scenes.

label: Synthesis and Checks
notes: Close by tying the algebra to runnable invariants from the notebook. The center sits in the null space, the block product reconstructs P up to scale, projection is scale invariant, and affine projection preserves parallel directions while perspective does not. Each claim is carried by a residual, not just by prose.
